column2: One should have a cow given at that holy place according to one's means; its whole fruit becomes imperishable, delight of Pandu.
Markandeya said: Then, king of kings, one should go to the excellent Naradeshvara, the supreme holy place among holy places, made by Narada.
Yudhishthira said: "Best of sages, for whom was the holy place made by Narada? Tell me all this, if you are pleased, excellent one."
Markandeya said: The blessed sage Narada, son of the supreme lord, practised austerity long ago on the northern bank of the Narmada.
By restraining the nine channels and attaining the state of a log, Narada pleased the glorious Mahadeva, Yudhishthira.
The Lord said: "I am pleased with you, chief of brahmins, lord of yogis, not born of a womb; ask a boon, divine one, whatever is in your mind."
Narada said: "By your grace, god, let yoga be perfected in me." The Lord said: "Let yoga be yours, and devotion to me alone at all times.
Go through existence moving at your own will, ranging over heaven and the netherworlds; you will roam the mortal world, yogi, and be hindered by no one.
The seven notes, three scales and twenty-one modulations, the divine dance and song dear to me, shall be yours as a yogi;
you will ever watch strife among gods, danavas and kinnaras; and your holy place on earth shall become holy by my grace."
Having said this, the god vanished, and Narada there installed the linga-bearer, king of kings, beneficial to all beings.
Markandeya said: An excellent holy place on earth was made by Narada; to that holy place, best of men, one should come with senses controlled.
In the lovely month of Bhadrapada, on the fourteenth of the dark fortnight, one should fast with supreme devotion and keep vigil at night.
An umbrella with auspicious marks should be given there to a brahmin; for those slain by weapons one should have shraddha performed;
by the power of the pinda offering they go to the supreme world. A tawny cow too should be given in that place, lord of men.

By the power of this shraddha of the brahmins, lord of men, of drinking the water of the Narmada and of wealth justly earned —
skandapuran:101:23	by the power of these may the departed go to the supreme goal. Uttering this, one should give a fee to the brahmin according to one's means,
and have sacrificial food given to the brahmins, wide-eyed one; by a single gift of learning an imperishable goal is attained.
Whoever at that holy place, king of kings, gives gold and sesame to a brahmin goes to heaven.
Markandeya said: Then, king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed pair of holy places, Dadhichchhanda and Madhuchchhanda, which destroy all sins.
A man who bathes at Dadhichchhanda and gives curd to a brahmin — this remains with him for seven births, O Bharata.
He has no disease, no old age, no grief and no envy; for a thousand months he is born in a great family.
At Madhuchchhanda, one who offers sesame water mixed with honey does not see the god Vaivasvata for seven births.
Whoever gives sesame mixed with honey, poverty never arises for his son or grandson.
Whoever gives sesame mixed with honey, whoever has a pinda offered mixed with honey,
whoever bathes at that holy place according to rule facing south — his father, grandfather and great-grandfather
are satisfied for sixteen years; there is no need for deliberation. Markandeya said: Then, king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Nanditirtha,
where Nandi attained perfection; I shall tell you all of it. Long ago Nandi, keeping the Narmada before him, practised austerity to Maheshvara
and reciting japa went from holy place to holy place; when he had passed Dadhichchhanda and Madhuchchhanda and was going on,
Mahadeva was pleased and said to Nandi. Maheshvara said: "O Nandisha, I am pleased; choose a boon as you wish.
I am pleased by this austerity and by the pilgrimage you have made." Nandi said: "I do not desire wealth, nor offspring for my family;
I do not desire liberation or anything else but your lotus feet, lord of gods. Among worms, insects and moths, among those gone into animal births,
in birth after birth may I go with unwavering devotion to you." Told "So be it" by the god, the supreme lord, Nandi
was quickly taken by the hand by Hara, who went to his abode. Whoever bathes at that holy place and worships the three-eyed one with devotion
obtains the holy fruit of the agnishtoma. Whoever gives up his life at that most holy place
becomes Shiva's follower and rejoices for an imperishable kalpa; then after a long time he is born in a great family,
knowing the truth of the Vedas and Vedangas, and lives a hundred autumns. This I have told you, son of Pritha, auspicious and giving all satisfaction,
rare, of true name, destroying all sins.
A man who bathes at that holy place, satisfies the ancestors and gods and worships Shankara with devotion goes to the supreme state.
A water-jar, a spouted pot or a large water vessel together with food, son of Pritha — hear the holy fruit of giving them:
whatever fruit a mortal gains from a twelve-year sacrificial session, he obtains that fruit; there is no need for deliberation.
Of all gifts the gift of food is unsurpassed, and whatever gives delight, and water, best of kings.
Men of cultivated self who die at that holy place dwell in Varuna's city until the deluge;
having enjoyed there for a long time, they are born in the mortal world; ever a giver of food, one lives a hundred autumns.
Markandeya said: Then, king of kings, one should go to the unsurpassed Agnitirtha, where the mighty Hutashana attained perfection by austerity.
He who was long ago made an all-devourer by a sage in the Dandaka forest — Hutashana, resorting to the bank of the Narmada, became purified.
A man who bathes at that holy place and worships the guru of the world together with Uma with devotion is freed from all sins.
A man who bathes at that holy place and gives gold, O king, and gives water to brahmins, obtains a fruit ten crores great.
At Dadhichchhanda, Madhuchchhanda, Nandisha, Varuna and Agneya — bathing, dear one, one gains that fruit and is freed from sins.
Worthy of salutation in the human world, blessed and with their wishes fulfilled are those who have seen the most holy five holy places of the Narmada;
they attain the world of heaven for as long as fourteen Indras reign; then, falling from heaven, they become righteous kings,
free of all sins, and enjoy the steadfast earth; such is the glory, equal to Indra's, of serving the bank of the Narmada.
The Ganga is holy at Kanakhala, the Sarasvati at Kurukshetra; but whether in a village or in the forest, the Narmada is holy everywhere.
Whoever lives always on the bank of the Reva and ever drinks its water has bathed at all holy places and drinks soma day after day.
The Ganga and all the other rivers, the oceans and the lakes, perish at the end of the kalpa; only the Narmada does not die.
Victory to the destroyer of Kama, who bears the Ganga on his head! Praised thus, Mahadeva became the giver of boons to the monkey.
The Lord said: "Ask a boon, child; say quickly what you ask." Hanuman said: "The sin of killing a brahmin has come upon me from slaying a brahmarakshasa, Maheshvara;
may I become sinless through speaking with you." The Lord said: "By the greatness of the holy places of the Narmada and the power of meditation and yoga,
and by seeing my form, you are at once sinless, no doubt." Having said this, the three-eyed god vanished together with Uma.
He installed Hanumadishvara there with devotion, by the power of his own yoga and the power of his celibacy;
by the Lord's power the wish-granting Shiva was installed, not to be cut, beyond reasoning, free of destruction and origin.
Markandeya said: There was a proof of old concerning Hanumadishvara, which happened at the beginning of the Dvapara and the end of the Treta, lord of men.
There was a royal sage on earth named Suparna; in his kingdom there was always happiness, and men were always long-lived.
He had a son, Shatabahu, of fearsome valour, ever devoted to japa and meditation, lord of men.
He roamed the whole earth, its mountains and forests, and came to the Vindhya mountain to hunt herds of deer,
crowded with kinds of deer, frequented by kinds of elephants, rich with the beauty of elephants and leopards, thronged with deer and boars.
Having sported there, the king sat down on a seat; then in the middle of the forest he saw a tawny-haired brahmin wandering.
The king said: "Why do you wander alone from forest to forest with a book in your hand, looking here and there? Tell me, best of the twice-born."
The brahmin said: "I have come from Kanyakubja, sent by a princess." The king said: "Tell me kindly for what purpose, lord."
The brahmin said: "King Shikhandi rules Kanyakubja; that lord of the earth had no son, and a daughter was born in answer to his wishes.
O king, she remembers her former birth and is of good conduct by the power of the Narmada. Her father said of that girl, when she was ready for marriage:
'In this worthless worldly existence I shall now give the gift of a daughter.' The girl said: 'At the time when I wish it, at that time let me be given.'
At his daughter's words the king was filled with wonder. Shikhandi said: 'Tell me, fortunate one, how you came to speak thus.'
At her father's word the girl bowed her head to the ground and told what had happened at Hanumadishvara, O king:
'I was a peahen, father, living with my mate near Urangamesha on the northern bank of the Reva.
In Hanuman's holy forest I used to sport as I pleased with my mate there, in a secluded vanjula and sarala tree.
Hunters came there to that excellent forest, tormented by hunger; by those sinners, who were angry with their master, I was slain together with my mate.
They wrung our necks and plucked us to eat; the hunters, laughing, quickly put us into the mouth of the fire,
roasted the flesh and ate as they pleased; they slept at night with contented senses, and the night came to an end.
The remains of that flesh were enjoyed by jackals, vultures and crows; a bone from my body, with sinew and flesh attached,
was then carried off by a bird flying through the sky; seeing the bird with flesh, other birds gathered,
and seeing the flock of birds it dropped the piece of bone; while all the birds ran after it and watched,
it fell into the water of the Narmada at Hanumadishvara, O king — my piece of bone fell into the water of the Narmada.
By the power of that holy place I was born in a kshatriya family; I was born a king's daughter with a face like the full moon.
I remember my former birth, lord of men; I was born in a kshatriya family. This I have told you, the whole cause, best of kings.
If for my sake you send someone, father, to that difficult place among the kinds of birds and beasts, to the water of the Narmada,
I shall tell him all the marks of the place.' Hearing the girl's words, Shikhandi said to me, O king:
'I will give you twenty villages; go to the bank of the Narmada.' My search was promised, though unseen and unforced.
'Go to the holy Narmada, which destroys all sins, to the auspicious Hanumadishvara, before Somanatha.
Half a krosha from the Reva, in a space wide with banyan trees and kadamba groves, in the chief part of the forest,
near a nyagrodha banyan, the bone will be seen as a mark. Gathering the earth and the bone, go to the Reva, best of the twice-born.
In the bright fortnight of Ashvina, on the day of the enemy of the Tripuras, bathe the trident-bearer with devotion and keep vigil at night;
at dawn cast it in quickly, standing navel-deep in the water; uttering this, best of the twice-born, a good goal comes to her.
Having cast in the bone, bathe again, which destroys sin.' What the girl told me I put all in the book.
I have come, best of kings, to that holy place, that great abode. Having seen the signs, I took up the bone, best of kings,
and by the rule stated before it was cast into the water of the Narmada. Then a rain of flowers fell, with 'Well done, well done, brahmin!'
Then a divine aerial car was seen at Hanumadishvara." Then the brahmin and the king both undertook a fast to death,
wasting themselves, devoted to worship of the Lord. As they meditated thus on the god — Shatabahu and the excellent brahmin —
after half a month the king, the wise Shatabahu, died; and an aerial car adorned with networks of little bells came there:
Well done, well done, best of kings; mount the aerial car. The king said: "I will not go by the upward path while the brahmin is not settled,
the excellent brahmin in the form of a guru, who gave me instruction." The gods said: "Men who die at Hanumadishvara, O king,
go to Shiva's world, which destroys all sin; but this brahmin's sin is not destroyed, lord of men,
for the brahmin still has house, wife and wealth." Then Shatabahu spoke to the brahmin with devotion:
Give up greed, the one root of adharma, best of the twice-born. Having said this, the king went to heaven with the dwellers in heaven.
After some days the brahmin went to heaven with the doers of good deeds; by the power of the holy place of the princess of Kashi's army,
given by his own daughter, the austerity earned in a former birth. On the eighth and fourteenth at all times, lord of sages,
and especially on the fourteenth of the dark fortnight in the month of Ashvina, one should bathe the Lord with devotion with honey, milk and ghee,
with curd mixed with sugar or with sesame water, and worship that Maheshvara with fragrant sandal;
then with fragrant flowers and bilva leaves — purifying — whoever has shraddha performed there by brahmins versed in the Veda,
endowed with all good marks, of good family, householders, should satisfy the brahmin with devotion with food, clothing and gold.
Let those in hell go to heaven, the twice-born should say; "let those in heaven go to the supreme world" — saying this, one should bow to the brahmins.
One should avoid fallen brahmins, one in whose house there is a vrishali: the woman who, leaving her own bull, acts as a cow with other bulls —
the gods know her as a vrishali; a shudra woman is not thereby a vrishali. The killing of a brahmin, the drinking of liquor, going to the guru's wife,
stealing gold, and what arises from betraying a friend — all these sins perish; so said Shankara.
What use is chatter, child, or saying much? Even one burdened with all sins should give a gift to an excellent brahmin.
The cow contains all gods and abides as the self of all gods; at the tips of her horns, lord of the earth, Shakra dwells always;
Hari is in her shoulder, Brahma in her head, the bull-borne god in her forehead; the moon and sun are to be known as her eyes, and Sarasvati in her tongue;
the hosts of Maruts and the Sadhyas are always her limbs, lord of men; Om, the four Vedas with the six Vedangas, the pada and krama texts,
the sages are in the pores of her hair, and the great mountains are known as her bones; the dark one with staff in hand, of great body, borne by a buffalo,
stands ever on her back, watching good and evil; the four holy oceans are the streams of milk in her udders;
the Ganga, born of Vishnu's body, removes sin by her sight; since she is thus constituted, she is always regarded by the wise...
and Lakshmi is in her dung, pure and wholly auspicious; therefore smearing with cow dung should be done, delight of Pandu.
Gandharvas, apsarases and the Ganga dwell in the cow's hooves; the Ashvins, sons of the Sun, are ever in her ears;
all the holy places on the earth bounded by the ocean, son of Pandu, are always present in the feet of cows.
Yudhishthira said: "Cows are equal to all holy places and adorned by the gods; tell me this, dear one: why have they taken refuge in cows?"
Markandeya said: Vishnu contains all gods, and cows are born from Vishnu's body; therefore they are to be given and always revered, as ordained by the wise.
White or tawny, giving milk, delight of Pandu — of all, the milk-giving cows covered with white cloth,
with bronze milking pails, adorned with golden horns, should be given; one should have them given with devotion to brahmins before Hanumadishvara.
She should be given in the natural way by one who desires heaven for himself; Yama has no power over them, and they go to Vishnu's world.
Falling from Vishnu's world, he goes to a brahmin's house and is born there a learned son, endowed with wealth.
The auspicious Hanumadishvara is a holy place that removes all sin; whoever hears of it is freed from the sin arising from mixture of castes;
whoever thinks of it on the new-moon day is freed, no doubt.
Soma went to the Grandsire trembling and bowed: "Brahma-born one, salutation to you; womb of the Vedas, salutation to you."
Brahma said: "The Reva is hard to reach everywhere, and especially in three places, O Bharata: at Omkara, at Bhrigukshetra and at Urageshvara."
Soma stood like a log meditating on the supreme Lord; when a full hundred years had passed, Maheshvara was pleased
and became manifest to Somanatha, seated on the bull, with Uma as half his body. Prostrating with eight limbs: "Victory, god, salutation to you!

Victory, Shankara, destroyer of the sinful, salutation; victory, Lord, master, salutation, salutation; victory, lord of beings adorned with Vasuki; victory to the bearer of trident and skull, salutation.

Victory, destroyer of Andhaka's body, salutation; victory to the slayer of the danavas' bodies, salutation; victory to the partless and the whole, salutation; victory to the subduer of time's portions, salutation.
Victory, blue-throated husband of Uma; victory, subtle, stainless Word, salutation; victory, first, beginningless, endless, salutation; victory, bearer of Pinaka and trident in hand, salutation."
Praised thus by Somanatha, son of Pandu, Mahadeva was pleased with him, best of kings, Shankara together with Uma.
The Lord said: "Choose a boon — blessings on you — whatever is in your mind." Soma said: "I am burned by Daksha's curse and my body has wasted, Maheshvara;
bring about the full calming of my sin, god." Maheshvara said: "I am captured by your devotion and pleased, together with Uma;
Somanatha has become sinless through serving the holy place." Having said this, the god vanished, and Soma, after meditating a moment, O king,
installed a linga granting perfection to living beings on earth, the god who removes all sorrow and destroys the killing of a brahmin.
Markandeya said: I shall tell you briefly the power of Somanatha. There was a king named Shambara; his son was Trilochana.
Trilochana's son was Kantha, devoted to sin, most vile. As he roamed in the forest a herd of deer was seen;
the whole herd of deer was slain by Trilochana's son. A brahmin in the form of a deer was moving among them in the lonely forest;
that best of sages was then slain by Kantha with a weapon. Laden with the killing of a brahmin, Kantha wandered the earth, his lustre gone.
Wandering, he reached the confluence of the Narmada and the Naga, crowded with kadamba and patala, adorned with bilva and orange trees,
with tamarind and champaka, beautified with agasti trees, with intoxicated bees, beautiful everywhere,
with leopards, deer, wildcats, lions and boars everywhere, with hares and gayals, resounding with the cries of peacocks.
Kantha entered that forest, tormented by thirst and worn by fatigue; he bathed in the holy water of the Reva at the confluence that destroys sin,
eating various leaves with his servants, and slept in the shade of a tree, tired from killing deer.
He worshipped Somanatha with supreme devotion, Yudhishthira, having drunk the water up to his throat, which destroys all sins.
Meanwhile a brahmin was going to the confluence to bathe at that best of holy places; the brahmin on the road, his mind set on it,
saw a single terrifying woman who had climbed a tree by the road; she said to the brahmin, "Stop, stop, best of the twice-born!"
Frightened, he looked in all directions, lord of men, and then saw the woman seated in the tree, clad in red garments,
a young woman wearing red flowers, anointed with red sandal, rich with the beauty of red ornaments, with a noose in her hand.
The woman said: "Hear my message, brahmin, if you are going to the confluence: my husband is staying there; send him away quickly.
Your wife is staying alone in the middle of the forest." Hearing this, the brahmin went to the confluence, rare even for the gods,
and the brahmin saw Kantha resting in the shade of a tree. The brahmin said: "At the forest's edge I saw a young woman with lotus eyes,
slender, wearing red garments, anointed with red sandal, with red garlands, richly adorned, noose in hand, doe-eyed;
seated in a tree she said, 'Send my husband to me.'" Kantha said: "In what place does the doe-eyed woman stay, chief of brahmins?
Whose is she and for what purpose? Tell me all this." The brahmin said: "Half a krosha from the confluence, at the lovely edge of the garden,
there that woman stays, her mind full of longing, lord." Then King Kantha said this to a servant, Yudhishthira:
Go and ask, 'Who are you, where have you come from and where will you go?' Then he went quickly to where the woman was,
saw the young woman in the tree and said, best of kings: "The king asks you, young woman: who are you and where will you go?"
The woman said: "The guru is the ruler of the self-controlled, the king the ruler of the wicked, and here Yama, son of Vivasvat, is the ruler of those with hidden sins.
The killing of a brahmin has come upon him from slaying a brahmin in the form of a deer; though joined with me, the king has been freed by the power of the holy place.
Within half a krosha of here the killing of a brahmin cannot enter; by the power of Somanatha the holy place is equal to Varanasi.
Go, and send Kantha to me quickly, without doubt." He told the whole story to the king.
At his words the king fell to the ground. The servant said: "Why do you grieve, master? Good and evil were born before."
Hearing his words, the king said this: "I shall give up my life here near Somanatha.
Quickly bring fire and plenty of firewood." At once everything was brought by his obedient servants.
Having bathed in the lovely water at the confluence that destroys sin, and worshipped Somanatha with supreme devotion, lord of men,
and having circumambulated the blazing fire three times, King Kantha entered it, keeping Janardana in his heart,
the god wearing yellow garments and a great crown: "By meditation on Vishnu, right here, may a good goal be mine."
A rain of flowers fell, with "Well done, well done, prince!" Seeing the incomparable wonder, they looked at one another,
and the servants offered themselves into the fire, meditating on the mace-bearer in their hearts; seated in aerial cars they all went together to heaven, delight of Pandu.
Markandeya said: This is the power of Somanatha; hear with one mind, O king. On the eighth and fourteenth at all times, on an auspicious day,
especially in the bright fortnight, and on a seventh falling on Sunday, the man who fasts with devotion should keep vigil at night,
bathe the supreme Lord with the five nectars and cow's products, anoint him with sandal and offer flowers, incense and the like,
light a lamp with ghee and have song and dance performed. On an eighth falling on Monday, at dawn, one should honour a brahmin
who is self-possessed, has conquered anger, avoids reviling brahmins, lovely in all limbs, tranquil, guarding his own wife,
reciting the Gayatri and ever free of wrong deeds. One in whose house lives a remarried woman, a vrishali or a shudra woman,
those with missing or extra limbs, those whose ancestry is unknown — such brahmins are always to be avoided by the wise at vows, shraddha and gifts.
A brahmin whose young wife is unchaste and who neglects Vedic study drags the giver down with himself, son of Pandu.
Brahmins devoted to their own dharma are like a boat of shalmali wood; they carry both the giver and themselves across.
Whatever man performs shraddha at Someshvara, son of Pritha, his ancestors are satisfied until the deluge.
Whoever gives food, clothing and gold to a brahmin goes to Shankara's world; this I say in truth.
Whoever gives a horse there furnished with full ornaments, red or yellow in colour and bearing all good marks,
its limbs smeared with saffron, and gives one without offspring, adorned with garlands at the neck and covered with white cloth,
saying "Place your foot on its shoulder and mount my horse," and when the brahmin has mounted, "May the Sun be pleased" —
he goes to Shankara's world free of all sins, and falling from that world he becomes a righteous king;
in his line the kingship never perishes; a long-lived son is born to him and an obedient wife;
he lives a hundred years and more, free of all sorrows. Whoever goes there at an eclipse of the moon with senses controlled,
fasting and having conquered anger, should give a cow to a brahmin — with her calf, full of milk, white, strong,
spotted, yellow or grey with a dark neck, or tawny, with cloth, adorned with a bell and ornaments,
with silver hooves, a bronze milking pail and golden horns, lord of men. By a white cow the lineage increases, a red one increases good fortune,
a spotted or copper-coloured one is declared to destroy sorrow, and a tawny one removes sin earned over three births.
He attains the world of that god and of Mandhatri, lord of people. At the end of a fortnight, at vyatipata, vaidhriti and the sun's transit,
at the gajachchhaya at day's end and at an eclipse of the sun, those who go with purified limbs to Vairanchya, rare even for the gods —
even the killer of his mother, the killer of his guru, and especially the killer of himself, should daily recite the "drupadad" and the others, and pranayama, O king,
and the Gayatri, whether Vaishnava, solar or Shaiva, as he pleases; he too is freed from sins — so said Shankara.
Whoever there circumambulates Somanatha has circumambulated Jambudvipa, lord of men.
The killing of a brahmin, drinking of liquor, going to the guru's wife — even the killer of an embryo is purified there, just so, no doubt.
Whoever with senses controlled hears this holy account of the holy place — even one sick with consumption obtains incomparable prosperity;
one seeking a son obtains a son, and one without desire attains heaven; hearing of this excellent holy place one is freed from all sins, O king.
All this I have told you, the fruit of Somanatha.
Pingaleshvara was installed by Havyavaha, king of kings. Yudhishthira said: "How was the Lord installed by Havyavaha, chief of brahmins?"
Markandeya said: When Havyavahana was sated with Rudra's seed, he obtained a body from the gentle Rudra and went away.
When it was cast into the mouth of Havyavaha by Rudra of boundless radiance, burned by Rudra's radiance he made a pilgrimage to the holy places.
Hutashana practised fierce meditation with supreme devotion; Hutashana lived on air for over a hundred years,
and then Mahadeva was pleased and said to Hutashana: "Havyavaha, name the boon that is in your mind."
Hutashana said: "Salutation to you, lord of all worlds, salutation to you of fierce form; scorched by your seed I have become hunchbacked, Maheshvara.
Afflicted in body and blackened, I stay on the bank of the Narmada." Saying "You will be free of disease," the god vanished.
Pingaleshvara was installed by Havyavaha, king of kings. Whoever, having conquered anger, keeps a fast there
obtains there the fruit of the atiratra and at the end attains Rudra. Whoever gives there a tawny cow to a virtuous but needy brahmin, O Bharata,
adorned, with cloth, with her calf and lovely to look at, goes to the supreme state.
Then, king of kings, one should go to a supremely lovely holy place, established by hosts of sages and brahmins born of Brahma's line,
renowned as Rinamochana, lying on the bank of the Reva. The man who for six months satisfies his ancestors there with devotion
is at once released from the debts to the gods, the ancestors and men, together with debts he has incurred himself, by bathing in the water of the Narmada.
There sin is seen manifest, even in bodily form. Whoever at that holy place, O king, single-minded and with senses controlled,
the wise man intent on devotion, has bathing and giving performed, is freed from the three debts and rejoices in heaven, full of vigour.
Markandeya said: Right after it, son of Pritha, is the excellent Kapilatirtha, established by Kapila himself, destroying all sins.
On the eighth and fourteenth of the bright fortnight, lord of men, one should bathe with supreme devotion, with the milk and ghee of a tawny cow,
with honey mixed with sugar, with curd, unbroken rice and fruit, Kapilesha, best of kings, the lord of the world, at midnight;
one should coat Maheshvara with fragrant sandal, and then with fragrant white flowers, delight of kings.
Those who worship thus, having conquered anger, do not go to Yama's abode; the dreadful sword-leaf forest and the most cruel creeper of Yama
they pass through at ease, son of Pritha, when Kapilesha is well worshipped. Bathing in the holy water of the Reva, one should honour a good brahmin
with the gift of a cow, with clothing and with food, O Bharata; by the gift of an umbrella and a bed he becomes a king on earth,
free of disease, of keen radiance, with living sons, sweet of speech; enemies become friends, no doubt.
Shiva was well installed there, desiring the good of the worlds. Whatever man worships Shambhu there, delight of Pandu,
obtains all desires and does not go to Yama's abode. On the dark eighth and the fourteenth, all desires are fulfilled, lord of men;
those who worship Mahakala do not go to Yama's abode.
It is renowned on earth under the name Jalashayi; having slain the danavas, Janardana slept there.
The discus was washed there by the god of gods, Shauri, and Sudarshana became sinless by the power of the Reva's water.
Yudhishthira said: "Tell me of Chakratirtha, frequented by hosts of sages, the incomparable power of Vishnu and the fruit of the Reva."
Markandeya said: Well done, well done, fortunate one! By Vishnu, Yudhishthira, the discus-bearer himself, a holy place more secret than the secret was made.
I shall tell you that story which destroys sin. Long ago there was a great daitya known as Nalamegha;
by him all the gods were defeated and their kingdoms taken, lord of men. Out of fear of Nalamegha, son of Pritha, Vishnu and the Rudras with Vasava,
Yama, Skanda, the lord of waters, Agni, the winds and the lord of wealth, the Vasus, the lord of speech, the Siddhas, Prachetas and the Grandsire —
the gods went to the supreme world saluted by Vishnu and Rudra; the gods headed by the lord of speech praised him with many kinds of hymns:
Salutation to you whose form is auspicious, pure self before creation, who afterwards took on distinctions by dividing the three gunas.
Seeing Indra and the other chief gods pale, lord of the earth, the god, inclined to grace, replied to the dwellers in heaven:

Welcome, hosts of gods; your former lustre has vanished, and the faces of the luminaries are like lotuses scorched by frost.
skandapuran:106:16	This weapon of the gods has been forcibly robbed of its flames; the thunderbolt of the slayer of Vritra looks as if its glory were blunted.
skandapuran:106:17	And this noose in the hand of Prachetas, hard for enemies to withstand, has become wretched, like a serpent whose power is taken by a spell.
skandapuran:106:18	Kubera's arm, its bracelet cast off, like a tree with broken branches, seems to proclaim the defeat that is a dart in his mind.
skandapuran:106:19	Yama too scratches the ground with his staff, its lustre gone; weary of his body, he goes into insignificance.
skandapuran:106:20	And these twelve Adityas, cooled by the loss of their glory, have become easy to look at, as if painted in a picture.
skandapuran:106:21	The creation of the worlds rests in me, their protection in you. Then with his thousand eyes, lovely as a lotus pond stirred by a gentle breeze,
the slayer of Vritra urged on his guru — the guru whose two eyes and Hara's three surpass a thousand eyes.
The lord of speech, with joined palms, said this to the swan-borne Brahma: "Born of your own line, dear one, is the mighty Nalamegha;
by that danava all the hosts of gods have been cast out. Nalamegha cannot be slain, hence I have come with the gods, shaken;
without the god Madhava he cannot be overcome. Holder of conch, lotus and mace, victory, bearer of the discus, lord!"
Hearing this praise by the gods, the one who lies on the waters awoke and spoke sweet words in a voice deep as a cloud:
Why have I been awakened, Brahman, by all the gods and asuras? Brahma said: "Out of fear of Nalamegha we have come to your abode.
The sinner Nalamegha cannot be slain by anyone, Janardana; the wicked one will meet death by your hand and not otherwise."
Janardana said: "Let the gods go to their own places; I shall slay the mighty one. Let the gods tell me the place where the evil-minded one lives."
The gods said: "The lord of the danavas lives in a cave of the Himalaya, Krishna, surrounded by twenty-four thousand maidens;
his horses and chariots are beyond counting, and his wondrous palaces are countless and many;
elephants like mountains and horses like elephants — the mighty one lives there, bringing fear to the gods."
Hearing the words of those distressed gods, the god called to mind Garuda, the render of hosts of foes.
Taking the discus in his hand, then mace and conch, the lord Janardana took up the Sharnga bow, the club and the plough,
and mounted the king of birds to slay the danava. In the danava's house, son of Pritha, portents dreadful to see appeared:
a jackal was in the middle of the house, a pigeon entered the house, and his banner staff fell without any wind;
there was a fight between snake and mouse and likewise between lion and elephant; the rivers there flowed off their courses, whirling;
trees on that mountain were seen flowering out of season. Then the lord of the world reached the Himalaya, king of mountains,
and Krishna blew the Panchajanya near the city; at the sound of the Panchajanya the lord of the danavas mounted his chariot.
Nalamegha said: "Who is this, come under the sway of death, wrapped in ignorance? Dhundhumara, go quickly, surrounded by your own army,
and bring that strong one before me by force, bound." Dhundhumara said: "I will bring him, no doubt, and the gods' partisans too, right now."
With his chariots, together with elephants, horses and soldiers, he saw, dear one, the source of the world, the mighty one seated on Suparna.
Seize him, seize him! said he to his servants; and Keshava's servants too were stationed in the four directions.
By Suparna and by the fire arrow they were slain like moths; Dhundhumara too was struck by Krishna with a blow of an arrow;
struck near the chest he fell on his chariot. Then all the danavas, ready for battle, cried out in dismay.
Then Nalamegha, enraged, came out mounted on his chariot and saw Keshava, son of Pritha, bearing conch, discus and mace.
Nalamegha said: "Kill Krishna, danavas, by whom the danava was slain! Having slain the chief of my army, where will he go now?"
Having said this, the danava assailed him with arrows, son of Pritha; Keshava cut down the danava's arrows there,
and Garutmat devoured that most terrible army. Krishna sent twice as many arrows there;
the danava doubled the double and sent them back; and they, eightfold, covered Krishna with their force.
Then the enraged god sent the fire weapon; Nalamegha released the Varuna weapon and in reply the wind weapon.
This Man-Lion sent the Narasimha weapon, son of Pandu; seeing the Narasimha weapon, the mighty Nalamegha
quickly got down from his chariot, took his sword in his hand and hurled it at Krishna to slay him, being the stronger.
Then the enraged danava came at Keshava, son of Pritha, and struck the mace-bearing Janardana with his sword.
Then Keshava, glad at heart, took up his sword and struck the mighty daitya Nalamegha in the chest.
Then the daitya struck Janardana with an iron shaft; Janardana, enraged, in battle against Nalamegha, O king,
took up his unfailing discus and struck off his head; with the fall of his head the earth trembled,
and the oceans, agitated, left their courses out of fear, son of Pritha. Then the gods rained down flowers upon Keshava.
He who could not be slain by the hosts of gods was slain by Keshava, and when Nalamegha was struck down the god went to his own place.
Janardana too, son of Kunti, resorted to the bank of the Narmada; Krishna, together with Lakshmi, disappeared on the bank of the Narmada.
The discus, stained, was released to wash away its sin, and fell into the water of the Narmada at Jalashayi;
its impurity was shaken off by the power of the Narmada. Whatever sin arose from the slaying of Nalamegha, lord of men,
all of it was quickly washed away in the water of the Reva, O Bharata. From that time in this world it is Jalashayi on the earth,
and others call it Chakratirtha, destroying floods of many sins.
Hear with one mind, O king, the power of that holy place: as Ananta is among serpents and Janardana among the gods,
and Margashirsha among months, so the Narmada is holy among rivers. In the month of Margashirsha, in the bright fortnight, on the auspicious eleventh day,
men who go there free of desire and anger and bathe the beloved of Shri who lies on the serpent couch,
king of kings, with supreme devotion, with honey, milk and ghee, with jaggery mixed in water — Janardana, source of the world —
and those burdened with worldly sins who watch him being bathed go to the supreme world saluted by gods and asuras.
